title: Rupee Beer Launches Diwali Campaign Linking Diyas, Food and Beer
excerpt: The Portland-based Indian-inspired brewer's 'Light One. Pour One.' campaign pairs lighting a diya with sharing food and beer for Diwali 2026.
body:
• Rupee Beer, the Portland, Maine-based Indian-inspired brand, has launched “Light One. Pour One.”, its 2026 Diwali campaign celebrating the Festival of Lights.
  • The campaign pairs the lighting of a diya with pouring a beer and sharing food, framing Diwali around togetherness, generosity and hospitality.
  • Rupee was founded by brothers Van and Sumit Sharma to pair specifically with Indian and spice-driven cuisine, with a portfolio from Basmati Rice Lager to a non-alcoholic beer.
  • For readers celebrating in the US, the range includes a non-alcoholic option, so guests who do not drink alcohol can still take part in the toast at the festive table.

Rupee Beer has introduced “Light One. Pour One.”, a 2026 Diwali campaign that recasts the Festival of Lights around three simple acts: lighting a diya, pouring a beer and passing food to the people gathered around the table. The Portland, Maine brand, created to pair with Indian and other global cuisine, announced the campaign in a release carried by Brewbound and promoted the same day on BevNET’s press release wire.

The company describes Diwali as the most important Indian calendar holiday and says the campaign is aimed at a new generation of globally minded consumers who embrace their heritage while making traditions their own. The message, it says, is to come together, share generously and make room for everyone at the table.

A Campaign Built Around the Diya

A diya is a small traditional oil lamp made from clay, brass or silver, holding a cotton wick dipped in ghee or vegetable oil. Originating in South Asia, diyas symbolize enlightenment, wisdom and the triumph of light over darkness, the release explains. Rupee takes that symbolism literally: light one, then pour one.

The brand says the campaign celebrates the rituals that connect people to their roots while embracing new traditions created with friends, family and communities around the world. As Indian culture continues to influence food, fashion, travel and lifestyle globally, Rupee says it sees an opportunity to invite people from all backgrounds to experience Diwali through its defining values of light, generosity, hospitality and togetherness.

Food First, by Design

Food is central both to Diwali and to Rupee’s business model. Festive tables bring together regional dishes, family recipes, sweets and bold flavours, and Rupee says its beers were developed specifically to complement Indian cuisine and spice-driven dishes. The pitch is not beer alongside food as an afterthought, but beer brewed for the food.

That food-first portfolio is detailed in the brand’s recent expansion release on BevNET: a flagship Basmati Rice Lager described as light, crisp and exceptionally food-friendly; an India Pale Ale inspired by the historic connection between India and British brewing; a seasonal Mango Wheat Ale using India’s national fruit; a non-alcoholic beer; and Darjeeling Hard Tea, rooted in India’s chai and tea culture. The beers were developed by master brewer Alan Pugsley, a British-born brewer with more than 40 years of experience across more than 100 brands.

A Family Restaurant Story From Portland

Rupee was founded by brothers Van and Sumit Sharma, sons of Indian restaurateurs whose family has spent more than 50 years in the restaurant business across the world. Growing up in that business, the brothers saw Indian restaurants in the United States often limited to imported lagers that were not designed for food pairing and were not always consistently available year-round, according to the Tennessee release. After living in London and Australia, they returned to Portland during the pandemic and built Rupee to close that gap.

Since launching in 2020, the brand has grown from a regional concept into a nationally distributed label. Its October expansion into Tennessee, through distributor Ajax Turner in the Nashville area, took its footprint to 25 states, with the Basmati Rice Lager and India Pale Ale leading the launch there. The company positions itself as America’s leading Indian-inspired beer brand and says additional expansion is planned.

What It Means for Diwali Tables in the US

For Indian-American households, the campaign lands on familiar ground: Diwali gatherings are already built around shared dishes, sweets and an open door for friends and neighbours. Rupee’s addition is to treat the drink with the same intent as the menu — choosing a lager brewed for spice, or the non-alcoholic option for guests who do not drink, rather than defaulting to whatever is in the fridge.

The closing line of the campaign is an invitation rather than a sales pitch: this Diwali, do not just wish for light, be the light — light a little brighter, pour a little more generously and celebrate together. Whether the beer is Rupee or not, the underlying ritual it is selling is the one diaspora families already practice: gather, feed people well, and keep a place at the table for one more guest.
